title: How the Black Death Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Black Death (mid-1340s to about 1352) in Europe. They cover a 2006 Texas Tech study using stomata counts that linked the plague to a drop in atmospheric carbon dioxide, the disease's gruesome symptoms, the death toll (about a third of Europe), its likely origin in Central Asia and the Genoese trading post at Kafa, the Tartar army's corpse-flinging, the "Big Death" naming and mistranslation, the Paris College of Physicians' planetary-alignment explanation, smoke and miasma remedies, quarantine's origin in Venice, flagellants and persecution of Jews, economic and social effects, the link to modern science, and modern debates about whether bubonic plague (Yersinia pestis) was the cause. The episode closes with a listener mail about a listener's family mob history.

segments.title: Opening banter and choosing the topic
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about the show and the Black Death topic, and Josh explains he found a news hook in a 2006 study on the Little Ice Age.

segments.title: Little Ice Age and stomata carbon dioxide study
segments.summary: A University of Tennessee study counted leaf stomata to infer atmospheric carbon dioxide. CO2 fell after the 1350s, which the hosts link to fewer people tending farmland and more trees after the Black Death killed a large share of the population. The hosts also mention a genetic bottleneck in the UK.

segments.title: Death toll and symptoms
segments.summary: The hosts describe the scale of death, roughly a third of Europe's population, and the symptoms: buboes, black spots, purple splotches called God's tokens, fevers, delirium, vomiting, coughing blood, and open sores, with death often within days.

segments.title: Burial crisis and grim conditions
segments.summary: With so many deaths in a few days, bodies could not be buried in time or with services, and corpses piled up in streets, with dogs eating them.

segments.title: Origins in Asia and the Kafa siege
segments.summary: The plague is said to have started in the Gobi Desert in the late 1320s and to have killed many in China. The Genoese trading post at Kafa was besieged by the Tartar army, which catapulted corpses over the walls. The Genoese fled to Sicily, and the disease spread into Europe along two routes.

segments.title: Naming the Big Death
segments.summary: The disease was first called the Big Death or Great Mortality. Later it came to be called the black death through a mistranslation of the Latin term, and the name stuck.

segments.title: Medieval theories, planetary alignment and remedies
segments.summary: The Paris College of Physicians blamed a planetary alignment producing a fog of death, or miasma. Remedies included burning aromatic wood, carrying rosemary, amber and musk, glass in southern windows, avoiding bathing, daytime sleep and sad thoughts.

segments.title: Origin of quarantine in Venice
segments.summary: Venice isolated arriving ships, first for thirty days and then for forty, giving the word quarantine. The hosts note that Venice still lost about a sixth of its population.

segments.title: Flagellants and persecution of Jews
segments.summary: The flagellants whipped themselves across Europe seeking to end the plague, turned against clergy and killed Jews, and were denounced by the Pope in 1349. Rumors that Jews poisoned wells led to mass killings, such as in Strasbourg in 1348.

segments.title: Social, economic and cultural effects
segments.summary: The plague caused labor shortages and higher wages, religious doubt, debauchery, the Dance of Death art theme, and a push toward physical science and new schools.
